authors: Gabríková K., Kachlík D., Belbl M. et al.

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.caption: A The accessory muscle head derived from the FPL muscle joining the regular muscle belly of the L1 muscle. B Scheme of the anomalous muscle head of the L1 muscle. L1 first lumbrical muscle, tAMHL1 tendon of the accessory muscle head of the first lumbrical muscle, AMHL1 accessory muscle head of the first lumbrical muscle, FPL flexor pollicis longus muscle, Asterisk tendinous interconnection between the FPL muscle tendon and the aberrant tendon
figures.what_it_shows: Palmar dissection (A) and scheme (B): an accessory muscle head from FPL whose tendon (tAMHL1) passes through the carpal tunnel to join the first lumbrical; asterisk/star marks the tendinous interconnection with the FPL tendon.
figures.labels_visible_in_image: L1, tAMHL1, AMHL1, FPL, four-point star; A, B

key_findings: Case report (formalin-embalmed Central European cadaver). Literature cited in text: 'The prevalence of the Linburg-Comstock variation is moving around 21% as reported by Yammine'; first-lumbrical variations 'occur in 17.3%' (Mehta and Gardner).
clinical_relevance: 'Such variation has a clinical significance ranging from the functional limitation of the thumb and index finger movement to the potential median nerve compression.'
notes: Surg Radiol Anat article that IS CC BY 4.0 (bucket licence_code CC BY). Only a case, but no OA original series on Linburg-Comstock was found (Thai 130-limb series and PMC8590423 reverse-LCV not usable: PMC8590423 has no licence).

topic: Bifid median nerve and persistent median artery on ultrasound (prevalence)
title: Sonographic Findings of the Bifid Median Nerve and Persistent Median Artery in Carpal Tunnel: A Preliminary Study in Chinese Individuals
authors: Chen L., Chen J., Hu B. et al.

figures.label: Figure 1 and Figure 2
figures.caption: Transverse ultrasonographic image (left side) and corresponding outline-marked image (right side) of a bifid median nerve (thin arrow) and PMA (thick arrow) at the level of the proximal carpal tunnel. Different PMA positions in relation to the median anatomy and a bifid median nerve with an intermediate position in relation to the PMA were most frequently observed.
figures.what_it_shows: Paired transverse ultrasound images (raw and outlined) at the proximal carpal tunnel showing bifid median nerve trunks (arrowheads/outlines) with a persistent median artery (thick arrow) in different positions, including colour Doppler.
figures.labels_visible_in_image: white outlines, thick arrows, triangular arrowheads; red Doppler signal; no text

key_findings: 160 wrists. 'a bifid median nerve was observed in 15 (9.4%) wrists, and a persistent median artery was observed in 12 (7.5%) wrists.' 'the probability of coexistence (6.3%) was higher than the probability of existing independently (bifid median nerve only 3.1%, persistent median artery only 1.3%).' 'Persistent median vein was observed in 9 wrists (5.6%).'
clinical_relevance: 'Their positional relationship in carpal tunnel is uncertain, and thus, preoperative ultrasound is necessary. These three variations do not present any additional risk for the development of carpal tunnel syndrome.'
notes: Complements repo entry PMC10343151 (persistent median artery). XML label is 'Figure 1 and Figure 2' (two figures in one image).

topic: Accessory abductor digiti minimi overlying Guyon's canal on ultrasound
title: Unveiling Guyon’s Canal: Insights into Clinical Anatomy, Pathology, and Imaging
authors: Saran S., Reddy P. S., Shirodkar K. et al.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Axial Gray-scale Ultrasound image at the level of the proximal Guyon’s canal, at the level of the pisiform bone, demonstrates an anatomical variant where an accessory abductor digiti minimi muscle (aADM) overlies the canal. The ulnar nerve (UN) is present within the canal, while the ulnar artery (UA) is positioned volar to the accessory muscle.
figures.what_it_shows: Axial ultrasound at the pisiform: an accessory abductor digiti minimi muscle belly lying superficial to the ulnar nerve within Guyon's canal, with the ulnar artery volar to it.
figures.labels_visible_in_image: UA, aADM, UN, Pisiform

key_findings: Review: describes the aADM as 'an anatomical variant in the hand, where an extra muscle lies adjacent to the ulnar nerve as it passes through Guyon's canal'; dynamic US during little-finger abduction distinguishes asymptomatic from compressive variants. No prevalence given in this article.
clinical_relevance: 'This dynamic evaluation is crucial for distinguishing between the asymptomatic presence of the accessory muscle and its pathological variant'.
notes: Prevalence figures (e.g. 22-35% in older cadaver/US series, Harvie 2004, Dodds 1990) are NOT in an OA article we could verify - do not cite numbers from this entry.

key_findings: 30 wrists (15 fresh cadavers). 'By dissection, type 1, 2 and 3 variants were found in 84%, 3%, and 13% of wrists'. 'extra-, sub-, and transligamentous courses were recorded in 65%, 31%, and 4% of cases'. Ultrasound vs dissection agreement 'kappa =0.9' for variant type and 'kappa =1' for MBMN course; 'the bifid nerve, hypertrophic muscles, and bilateral symmetry ... 13.3%, 13.3%, and 86.7%'.
clinical_relevance: 'Ultrasound can be used reliably to identify anatomic variations of the MN and MBMN. It could be a useful tool before carpal tunnel release surgery.'
notes: Image labels write 'BM' where caption says 'MB' (motor branch). Each figure combines a cadaver photo (also usable in topo slides) with US.
